questions.q: What does TypeScript check when you pass a value to a parameter of type Payment?
questions.explain: TypeScript is structurally typed: compatibility is decided by shape, not by name or origin. Extra members are allowed (outside of fresh literals), which is how an Order with an id and an amountKobo passed as a Payment.
options: That the value was created with the name Payment
That the value has every required member of Payment, each with a compatible type
That the value has exactly the members of Payment, no more and no fewer
That the value is an instance of a class called Payment

questions.q: Why is TypeScript structural rather than nominal?
questions.explain: TypeScript had to describe JavaScript as it is written. Objects rarely declare a type at creation, so the only thing the compiler can compare is their shape.
options: Structural checking is faster to compile
JavaScript objects are mostly plain literals passed between libraries, and duck typing is how existing JavaScript works; a nominal system would reject most of it

questions.q: Two classes, PaymentId and OrderId, each have exactly one member: #value: string. Can an OrderId be passed where a PaymentId is expected?
questions.explain: The compiler cannot compare members it cannot see from outside, so private members make a class behave nominally. It is a real technique, with the runtime cost of an object per id.
options: Yes, they have the same shape
No: classes with private or #private members are only compatible with themselves and their subclasses
Only if both classes are exported from the same file

questions.q: Inside structural typing, what is the simplest change that stops an Order being accepted as a Payment when both have id and amountKobo?
questions.explain: Different literal types are incompatible, so the shapes no longer match. Names and type versus interface do not matter structurally, and readonly properties do not affect assignability.
options: Declare Payment as a type instead of an interface
Give each a literal discriminant, such as kind: "payment" and kind: "order"

questions.q: Given interface Payment { readonly amountKobo: number } and interface Editable { amountKobo: number }, what does const e: Editable = payment; do?
questions.explain: This is a known hole: readonly arrays are checked in assignments, readonly properties are not. The assignment creates an alias, not a copy, so writing through it changes the original.
options: Fails with TS4104, like readonly arrays
Compiles: readonly on a property does not affect assignability, so the payment can then be changed through e
Copies the payment so the original stays safe

questions.q: A function takes options: { reason?: string; notifyCustomer?: boolean }. You pass a variable holding { notify: true }. What happens?
questions.explain: A type whose properties are all optional is a weak type. Assigning something that shares none of its properties is almost certainly a mistake, so TypeScript reports it, even for a variable that is not a fresh literal.
options: It compiles, because every property of the options type is optional
TS2559: the type has no properties in common with the weak type
TS2353: an excess property check on notify

questions.q: In which of these does an excess property check run on { paymentId: "PAY-1", amountKobo: 500, reasn: "late" }?
questions.explain: Only a fresh literal, written where the target type is known, is checked. Variables, spread properties and parsed JSON all pass extra properties through silently.
options: When the literal is stored in an unannotated const first and then passed to the function
When it is spread into the argument: requestRefund({ ...saved })
When the literal is written directly as the argument: requestRefund({ … })

questions.q: With type Payout = { last4: string } | { bank: string }, does const p: Payout = { last4: "4242", bank: "GTBank" } compile?
questions.explain: The literal is a valid { last4: string } with a property that another member knows, so it passes. Add a kind discriminant and TypeScript checks the literal against the chosen member alone.
options: No, bank is excess for the card member
Yes: for a union without a discriminant, a property is only excess if no member has it
No, an object cannot match two members of a union
Yes, but bank is removed at runtime

questions.q: A sign-up handler types its body as { name: string; email: string }. An attacker sends "role": "admin" in the JSON. What stops the extra field?
questions.explain: Types are erased and the body comes from JSON.parse, which is never a fresh literal. Unknown keys survive unless a runtime validator strips or rejects them.
options: Only runtime code that removes or rejects unknown keys

questions.q: A generic type F<T> is covariant in T when…
questions.explain: Covariance keeps the direction of subtyping. It is safe when T only comes out of the type: return values, readonly arrays, promises.
options: F<PaidOrder> is assignable to F<Order>, in the same direction as PaidOrder to Order
Neither is assignable to the other
F has more than one type parameter

questions.q: Which of these types is contravariant in T?
questions.explain: A function that accepts a T only consumes it. A handler for any Order can serve as a handler for PaidOrder, not the reverse: the direction flips.

questions.q: Why is type Slot<T> = { get: () => T; set: (value: T) => void } invariant?
questions.explain: Widening a Slot<PaidOrder> to Slot<Order> would let set store an unpaid order; narrowing the other way would let get return an order without paidAt. Only exact matches are safe.
options: Because it is a type alias, not an interface
T comes out of get and goes into set, so each direction of assignment breaks one of them

questions.q: Mutable arrays are treated as covariant, which is unsound. Why did the TypeScript team choose it?
questions.explain: It is a deliberate trade of soundness for convenience. The defence is to take arrays you only read as readonly T[], where covariance is sound because there is no push.
options: They did not know about the problem
Invariant arrays would reject a lot of correct code, such as passing string[] to a function that reads (string | number)[]

questions.q: An interface declares handle(event: ShopEvent): void, and an object whose handle only accepts PaymentCaptured compiles against it. What change makes the compiler reject that object?
questions.explain: Method parameters are checked bivariantly even in strict mode. Function-typed properties get the strict, contravariant check.
options: Declare the member as a function-typed property: handle: (event: ShopEvent) => void

questions.q: Why does TypeScript keep method parameters bivariant?
questions.explain: If push's parameter were checked strictly, T would be in an input position and PaidOrder[] could no longer be used as Order[] anywhere. Method bivariance keeps the standard library convenient.
options: To make methods faster at runtime
Built-in types such as Array<T> use methods like push(...items: T[]); strict checks would make them invariant and break common code
Because methods cannot have type annotations

questions.q: Which compiler flag makes function-typed parameters contravariant instead of bivariant?
questions.explain: strictFunctionTypes applies to function types and function-typed properties, but not to method syntax, which stays bivariant.

questions.q: What does interface Feed<out T> { readonly latest: () => T } tell the compiler?
questions.explain: out means T only comes out of the type. If a member ever used T as an input, the annotation would fail with TS2636.
options: That T must be an object type
That T is covariant; the compiler checks the annotation against the structure and uses it instead of measuring variance
That T can only be used in output files
That the interface cannot be implemented by classes

questions.q: Which is not a benefit of in/out annotations?
questions.explain: An annotation that contradicts the structure is an error (TS2636). Annotations document and check; they do not loosen the rules.
options: They document the variance in a way the compiler checks
They catch a change that accidentally alters a type's variance
They can speed up checking of very large recursive generic types
They let you make an unsound variance compile, for example out on a type that consumes T

questions.q: In interface Channel<E> { readonly subscribe: (handler: (event: E) => void) => void }, in which direction does E flow through subscribe?
questions.explain: Each function parameter position flips the direction. E is a parameter of the handler, which is itself a parameter of subscribe, so the two flips cancel. The channel gives events out to handlers.
options: Out: it is a parameter of a parameter, which flips twice; the channel hands events to the handler
Both, so subscribe alone makes the type invariant
Neither: callbacks do not affect variance

questions.q: Which of these costs the compiler work every time it is used with a new type argument?
questions.explain: Recursive object and union types are descriptions, expanded lazily. A recursive conditional or mapped type that builds a result is a computation, repeated for each input.
options: interface Category { name: string; children: readonly Category[] }
type Json = string | number | boolean | null | Json[] | { [key: string]: Json }
type Paths<T> = { [K in keyof T & string]: T[K] extends object ? `${K}.${Paths<T[K]>}` : K }[keyof T & string]

questions.q: In type Reachable<S, Seen = never> = S extends Seen ? never : S | Reachable<Next<S>, Seen | S>, what makes the recursion stop at a final status such as "delivered"?
questions.explain: A final status has an empty list of next statuses, so the recursive call receives never, which distributes over zero members and produces never. Seen handles cycles, not final states.
options: Next<"delivered"> is never, and a distributive conditional type over never is never

questions.q: Why does type Otp = `${Digit}${Digit}${Digit}${Digit}${Digit}${Digit}` fail with TS2590?
questions.explain: Template literal types multiply their unions: 106 strings. The better design is string plus a runtime pattern check, with a brand to record that the check passed.
options: Template literal types cannot contain unions
It would be a union of a million members, and the compiler refuses unions larger than 100,000
Six placeholders exceed the recursion depth

questions.q: The lesson's Paths<T> is applied to { zones: { name: string }[] }. What does it produce?
questions.explain: Array indexes are numbers, so keyof T & string skips them; every method is a function, which extends object but yields no paths. Only length is left: a quiet wrong answer, the most dangerous kind.

questions.q: When is a type that computes its answer most likely worth keeping?
questions.explain: Outside data needs a runtime check anyway; one-off puzzles cost more to read than they save. Types like Awaited or an overloaded pipe earn their place by serving many callers well.
options: When it replaces a runtime check for data that comes from JSON
When it is used once, in one file, for one value
When it sits at a library boundary, catches a large class of mistakes, has readable errors and type tests, and stays cheap on realistic inputs

questions.q: The build's type test helper is type Assignable<From, To> = [From] extends [To] ? true : false. Why the brackets?
questions.explain: A naked type parameter in extends distributes: From = A | B would give true | false, which is boolean. Wrapping both sides in a one-element tuple asks the question once for the whole union.
options: They stop the conditional type from distributing over a union From, so the whole type is compared at once
Without them, never would be assignable to nothing
They turn the result into an array of booleans

questions.explain: all and paid are the same array. Covariant mutable arrays let an unpaid order into the "paid" list, and its paidAt is missing at runtime.
options: TypeError: Cannot add property 1, object is not extensible

questions.q: This compiles under strict. What does it print?
questions.explain: Method syntax is checked bivariantly, so the narrower implementation compiled. At runtime order.paidAt is undefined, and reading .length of it throws a TypeError.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A readonly property fits a mutable one, and the assignment makes an alias, not a copy. Nothing is frozen at runtime, so the write goes through.
options: TypeError: Cannot assign to read only property 'amountKobo' of object

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The variable is not a fresh literal, so there is no excess property check, and types never remove properties at runtime. The object keeps all three keys.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: JSON.parse returns any, and the annotation checks nothing at runtime. The attacker's role is still in the object. Only a runtime validator can strip it.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A function that returns a value fits a void function type; void only says the caller should not use the result. push still returned the new length, a number.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A function with fewer parameters fits a function type with more: it just ignores the extra arguments. recordSku.length is the number of declared parameters, 1.

questions.q: This compiles. What does it print?
questions.explain: A class with only public members is just a shape, so any object with those members fits, including one whose naira lies. instanceof sees the truth at runtime. A #private field would have made the literal a compile error.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A Handler<unknown> accepts anything, so it fits Handler<string> (contravariance). A Set stores each function once, so it runs once, and delete returns true when it removed something.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Properties that arrive through a spread are not excess-checked, so reasn survives. The explicit amountKobo comes after the spread, so it wins.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The seen set breaks the paid → pending cycle, exactly like the Seen accumulator in the type. archived points to pending, but nothing points to it, so it is unreachable. Breadth-first order visits paid and cancelled before refunded.
options: The loop never ends because of the cycle

questions.q:
Give Payment and Order a literal kind discriminant so they are no longer interchangeable, and finish refundAll: it refunds only the payments in a mixed list, skipping orders. The program should print:

refund 1638750 to PAY-88
skip ORD-1042
refund 500000 to PAY-90
questions.explain: With different literal kinds, an Order no longer fits a Payment, and checking kind narrows each item. A function typed (payment: Payment) would now reject an order at compile time.
questions.expected:
refund 1638750 to PAY-88
skip ORD-1042
refund 500000 to PAY-90

questions.q: Excess property checks do nothing for parsed JSON. Finish pickKnown(input, keys): return a new object with only the listed keys that are present as own properties of input. The program should print {"name":"Ada","email":"ada@example.com"}.
questions.explain: An allow-list copies only the keys you expect, so role never reaches your code. Object.hasOwn skips missing keys (no "phone": undefined) and ignores inherited ones.

questions.q:
Finish createChannel: publish calls every subscribed handler with the event, and subscribe returns a function that unsubscribes. Handlers are function-typed properties, so they are checked contravariantly. The program should print:

sms: PAY-88
audit: PAY-88
audit: PAY-90
questions.explain: A Set keeps handlers in insertion order and lets the returned closure remove exactly one. The in out annotation compiles because E goes into publish and out to each handler.
questions.expected:
sms: PAY-88
audit: PAY-88
audit: PAY-90

questions.q: The covariance bug came from pushing into an array through a wider alias. Finish withOrder(list, order) so it never mutates: it returns a new readonly list. The program should print 1 2 ORD-2.
questions.explain: A readonly list has no push, so covariance is sound: nobody can insert the wrong kind of order through a wider view. Adding means building a new list.

questions.q: Write the runtime twin of the Paths type: paths(value) returns every dotted path to a leaf of a nested settings object, where a leaf is anything that is not a plain object (arrays count as leaves). The program should print currency,delivery.freeAboveKobo,delivery.zones,payments.card.enabled.
questions.explain: At runtime you decide explicitly what a leaf is: arrays and null are handled in one readable line, where the type version needed extra branches. A debugger can step through this function; nobody can step through a type.

questions.q: Finish unreachable(flow, start): walk the transition table from start and return the statuses that are never visited, in table order. Guard against cycles. The program should print archived,disputed.
questions.explain: A depth-first walk with a stack works as well as the breadth-first queue: the set of visited statuses is the same. disputed leads to paid, but nothing leads to disputed. This test does the job of the Reachable type, with no compile-time cost.

questions.q: readonly types do not stop an alias or a cast from writing. Finish deepFreeze so the runtime refuses writes at every level, not just the top. The program should print true true true.
questions.explain: Object.freeze is shallow, so recurse into the children as well. Freezing the object alone would print true false false: the nested delivery object and the zones array could still be changed through any reference.

questions.q: Finish readSetting(settings, path): follow a dotted path through nested plain objects and return the value, or undefined as soon as a step is missing or is not an object. Use own properties only, so "toString" is not a setting. The program should print 100000 undefined undefined.
questions.explain: Each step narrows unknown to an object before indexing, and Object.hasOwn refuses inherited names. The result is unknown, honestly: the caller must check it. A computed Paths type could reject the typo at compile time, but only for paths written in code, and at the costs the lesson measured.
